1 Chronicles — Book introduction (Modern English production candidate)

The two books of Chronicles repeat much of the history found in Samuel and Kings.

Yet they also contain excellent and useful details that are recorded nowhere else.

The first book traces the Jewish people from Adam and then recounts the reign of David.

The second book continues the history of Judah's kingdom through its progress and decline, and also records the return of the Jews from Babylonian captivity.

Jerome said that people who think they understand the Scriptures without knowing Chronicles deceive themselves.

These books preserve events passed over in other accounts, genealogical names and connections between passages.

They also help explain many questions concerning the gospel.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesGenealogies, Adam to Abraham.1–27The descendants of Abraham.28–54
Genealogies from Adam to Abraham (verses 1–27)

This chapter and many that follow bring together genealogies—lists of parents and descendants—already found elsewhere in Scripture, while adding other details.

When we compare these lists with other passages, we may notice differences.

But those differences should not cause us to lose confidence in God's word.

We should instead thank him that the truths necessary for salvation are sufficiently clear.

This record traces the Jewish nation's ancestry to the first man created by God.

That makes it different from the obscure, legendary or absurd claims about national origins that have circulated elsewhere.

People of different nations have since become so mixed with one another that no present-day nation—or even most of its population—can be said to descend exclusively from a single ancient line.

One thing remains certain: God made all nations from one blood.

We are all descended from one Adam and one Noah.

Do we not all have one Father?

Has not one God created us? (Malachi 2:10)

Abraham's descendants (verses 28–54)

From this point onward, the genealogy concentrates on Abraham's descendants.

As we read so many names, we should think about the multitudes who have lived on earth, played their part in its history and then departed.

One generation passes, including generations of sinful people, and another comes after it (Ecclesiastes 1:4; Numbers 32:14).

This succession will continue as long as the earth remains.

Our own passage through time into eternity is very short.

May we be distinguished as people who truly belong to the Lord.
classic_reading:
[1Chr.1.1-1Chr.1.27]
1 Chronicles
The books of Chronicles are, in a great measure, repetitions of what is in the books of Samuel and of the Kings, yet there are some excellent useful things in them which we find not elsewhere. The FIRST BOOK traces the rise of the Jewish people from Adam, and afterward gives an account of the reign of David. In the SECOND BOOK the narrative is continued, and relates the progress and end of the kingdom of Judah; also it notices the return of the Jews from the Babylonish captivity. Jerome says, that whoever supposes himself to have knowledge of the Scriptures without being acquainted with the books of Chronicles, deceives himself. Historical facts passed over elsewhere, names, and the connexion of passages are to be found here, and many questions concerning the gospel are explained.
Chapter 1
Chapter Outline
Genealogies, Adam to Abraham. | (1-27) |
The descendants of Abraham. | (28-54) |
Verses 1-27
This chapter, and many that follow, repeat the genealogies, or lists of fathers and children in the Bible history, and put them together, with many added. When compared with other places, there are some differences found; yet we must not therefore stumble at the word, but bless God that the things necessary to salvation are plain enough. The original of the Jewish nation is here traced from the first man that God created, and is thereby distinguished from the obscure, fabulous, and absurd origins assigned to other nations. But the nations now are all so mingled with one another, that no one nation, nor the greatest part of any, is descended entirely from any of one nation, nor the greatest part of any, is descended entirely from any of these fountains. Only this we are sure of, that God has created of one blood all nations of men; they are all descended from one Adam, one Noah. Have we not all one father? Has not one God created us? Mal 2:10.
[1Chr.1.28-1Chr.1.54]
Verses 28-54
The genealogy is from hence confined to the posterity of Abraham. Let us take occasion from reading these lists of names, to think of the multitudes that have gone through this world, have done their parts in it, and then quitted it. As one generation, even of sinful men, passes away, another comes. [Eccl.1.4] Ec 1:4; [Num.32.14] Nu 32:14, and will do so while the earth remains. Short is our passage through time into eternity. May we be distinguished as the Lord's people.

modern_osis:
Original heading

Genealogies.

The families of Israel

We now come to the register of the children of Israel, the people set apart from the nations, who were to dwell as a distinct people and not be counted among other nations.

But in Jesus Christ, everyone who comes to him is welcome to his salvation.

All have equal privileges through faith in him, love for him and wholehearted devotion to him.

Everything truly valuable lies in God's favor, peace and likeness, and in a life dedicated to his glory by seeking the well-being of other people.
classic_reading:
[1Chr.2.1]
Chapter 2
Genealogies.
--We are now come to the register of the children of Israel, that distinguished people, who were to dwell alone, and not be reckoned among the nations. But now, in Christ, all are welcome to his salvation who come to him; all have equal privileges according to their faith in him, their love and devotedness to him. All that is truly valuable consists in the favour, peace, and image of God, and a life spent to his glory, in promoting the welfare of our fellow-creatures.

modern_osis:
Original heading

Genealogies.

David's descendants

Among all Israel's families, none was more distinguished than David's family.

This chapter gives a full account of that line.

Jesus Christ, as to his human ancestry, came from David's family.

Attentive readers will also notice how many advantages the children of the righteous enjoy.
classic_reading:
[1Chr.3.1]
Chapter 3
Genealogies.
--Of all the families of Israel, none were so illustrious as the family of David: here we have a full account of it. From this family, as concerning the flesh, Christ came. The attentive observer will perceive that the children of the righteous enjoy many advantages.

modern_osis:
Original heading

Genealogies.

Judah, Simeon, and the prayer of Jabez

This chapter gives additional family records for Judah, the largest and most famous of Israel's tribes, and also for Simeon.

The most remarkable person mentioned is Jabez.

Scripture does not tell us why he was more honorable than his brothers.

But it does show that he was a man of prayer.

True greatness comes through desiring to do God's will and praying earnestly.

Jabez prayed to the living and true God, the only One who can hear and answer.

In approaching God he recognized the Lord as the One who had made a covenant with his people.

Jabez did not state a promise of his own.

He left his commitment understood, unwilling to make assurances in his own strength, while sincerely desiring to dedicate himself entirely to God.

The attitude of his prayer can be expressed like this:

Lord, if you bless and preserve me, you may do whatever you will with me. I will remain at your command and disposal forever.

His prayer expressed a deep and affectionate longing for God's blessing.

It contained four requests.

First, that God would truly bless him. Spiritual blessings are best, because God's blessings are real and bring real results.

Second, that God would enlarge his territory. We should desire that the Lord enlarge our hearts, and thus increase our share in him and in the heavenly Canaan.

Third, that God's hand would be with him. God's hand guiding, protecting, strengthening and working in us and for us is entirely sufficient for all our needs.

Fourth, that God would protect him from evil. This includes the evil of sin, painful troubles and the harmful plans of enemies, so that such things would not injure him or make him truly a Jabez—a man of sorrow.

God granted what Jabez asked.

The Lord remains ready to hear prayer.

His ear is not too heavy to hear us now.
classic_reading:
[1Chr.4.1]
Chapter 4
Genealogies.
--In this chapter we have a further account of Judah, the most numerous and most famous of all the tribes; also an account of Simeon. The most remarkable person in this chapter is Jabez. We are not told upon what account Jabez was more honourable than his brethren; but we find that he was a praying man. The way to be truly great, is to seek to do God's will, and to pray earnestly. Here is the prayer he made. Jabez prayed to the living and true God, who alone can hear and answer prayer; and, in prayer he regarded him as a God in covenant with his people. He does not express his promise, but leaves it to be understood; he was afraid to promise in his own strength, and resolved to devote himself entirely to God. Lord, if thou wilt bless me and keep me, do what thou wilt with me; I will be at thy command and disposal for ever. As the text reads it, this was the language of a most ardent and affectionate desire, Oh that thou wouldest bless me! Four things Jabez prayed for. 1. That God would bless him indeed. Spiritual blessings are the best blessings: God's blessings are real things, and produce real effects. 2. That He would enlarge his coast. That God would enlarge our hearts, and so enlarge our portion in himself, and in the heavenly Canaan, ought to be our desire and prayer. 3. That God's hand might be with him. God's hand with us, to lead us, protect us, strengthen us, and to work all our works in us and for us, is a hand all-sufficient for us. 4. That he would keep him from evil, the evil of sin, the evil of trouble, all the evil designs of his enemies, that they might not hurt, nor make him a Jabez indeed, a man of sorrow. God granted that which he requested. God is ever ready to hear prayer: his ear is not now heavy.

modern_osis:
Original heading

Genealogies.

The tribes east of the Jordan

This chapter gives an account of the two and a half tribes that settled on the east side of the Jordan.

They were later taken captive by the king of Assyria because they had abandoned the Lord.

Only two events are highlighted in Henry's summary of their history.

First, they shared a victory.

Happy are people who live in harmony and help one another resist the common enemies of their souls, trusting the Lord and calling on him together.

Second, they shared captivity.

They had sought the best land, without considering that its position made it especially exposed to enemy attack.

Strong desires for earthly possessions can draw us away from God's appointed means of worship and prepare us for destruction.
classic_reading:
[1Chr.5.1]
Chapter 5
Genealogies.
--This chapter gives some account of the two tribes and a half seated on the east side of Jordan. They were made captives by the king of Assyria, because they had forsaken the Lord. Only two things are here recorded concerning these tribes. 1. They all shared in a victory. Happy is that people who live in harmony together, who assist each other against the common enemies of their souls, trusting in the Lord, and calling upon him. 2. They shared in captivity. They would have the best land, not considering that it lay most exposed. The desire of earthly objects draws to a distance from God's ordinances, and prepares men for destruction.

modern_osis:
Original heading

Genealogies.

Levi's descendants

This chapter records the descendants of Levi.

More than any other Israelites, the priests and Levites needed to preserve and be able to prove their ancestry clearly.

The honors and privileges of their priestly service depended on that descent.

Under the gospel, however, the Spirit of God calls ministers to service without limiting them to any particular family.

At the same time, both then and now, ministers and believers may be very useful to the church, but only our great High Priest, Jesus Christ, can make atonement for sin.

No one can be accepted by God except through Christ's atoning sacrifice.
classic_reading:
[1Chr.6.1]
Chapter 6
Genealogies.
--We have an account of Levi in this chapter. The priests and Levites were more concerned than any other Israelites, to preserve their descent clear, and to be able to prove it; because all the honours and privileges of their office depended upon their descent. Now, the Spirit of God calls ministers to their work, without any limit as to the families they came from; and then, as now, though believers and ministers may be very useful to the church, none but our great High Priest can make atonement for sin, nor can any be accepted but through his atonement.

modern_osis:
Original heading

Genealogies.

The missing records of Zebulun and Dan

This chapter contains no genealogical account of either Zebulun or Dan.

We cannot explain why only these tribes were omitted.

Yet it is a disgrace connected with Dan that idolatry began among its settlers in Laish, the city they renamed Dan (Judges 18).

Later, Jeroboam established one of his golden calves there.

Henry also notes that Dan is omitted from the tribal list in Revelation 7.

People become detestable when they abandon the worship of the true God in order to worship some created thing.
classic_reading:
[1Chr.7.1]
Chapter 7
Genealogies.
--Here is no account either of Zebulun or Dan We can assign no reason why they only should be omitted; but it is the disgrace of the tribe of Dan, that idolatry began in that colony which fixed in Laish, and called it Dan, Jud 18 and there one of the golden calves was set up by Jeroboam. Dan is omitted, Re 7. Men become abominable when they forsake the worship of the true God, for any creature object.

modern_osis:
Original heading

Genealogies.

Benjamin's family record

This chapter gives a longer genealogical account of the tribe of Benjamin.

Many details that now seem difficult, sudden or confusing probably made good sense to the original readers and fully served the purpose for which these records were written.

At that time, many great and powerful nations existed and many distinguished people were famous.

Their names have now been completely forgotten.

Yet the names of many ordinary people who belonged to the Israel of God remain permanently recorded here.

The memory of the righteous is blessed.
classic_reading:
[1Chr.8.1]
Chapter 8
Genealogies.
--Here is a larger list of Benjamin's tribe. We may suppose that many things in these genealogies, which to us seem difficult, abrupt, and perplexed, were plain and easy at that time, and fully answered the intention for which they were published. Many great and mighty nations then were in being upon earth, and many illustrious men, whose names are now wholly forgotten; while the names of multitudes of the Israel of God are here kept in everlasting remembrance. The memory of the just is blessed.

modern_osis:
Original heading

Genealogies.

The people who returned from Babylon

One purpose of preserving these genealogies was to guide the Jews returning from captivity.

The records helped them identify which people to join and where to live.

The chapter also describes the good order restored to the work of worship after the return from Babylon.

Everyone knew the duty entrusted to them.

Work is more likely to be done well when people know the responsibilities of their own position and take them seriously.

God is a God of order.

The earthly temple thus pictured the heavenly sanctuary, where worshipers never cease praising God day or night (Revelation 4:8).

Blessed be his name!

In heaven believers will praise him not in rotating shifts, but all together and without interruption, day and night.

May the Lord make each of us fit to share the inheritance of the saints in light.
classic_reading:
[1Chr.9.1]
Chapter 9
Genealogies.
--This chapter expresses that one end of recording all these genealogies was, to direct the Jews, when they returned out of captivity, with whom to unite, and where to reside. Here is an account of the good state into which the affairs of religion were put, on the return from Babylon. Every one knew his charge. Work is likely to be done well when every one knows the duty of his place, and makes a business of it. God is the God of order. Thus was the temple a figure of the heavenly one, where they rest not day nor night from praising God, [Rev.4.8] Re 4:8. Blessed be His name, believers there shall, not in turn, but all together, without interruption, praise him night and day: may the Lord make each of us fit for the inheritance of the saints in light.

modern_osis:
Original heading

The death of Saul.

Saul's death and the way opened for David

A major purpose of Chronicles appears to be preserving the history of David's family.

That is why the writer does not repeat Saul's whole reign.

He records only Saul's death, which opened the way for David to become king.

Henry draws three lessons from Saul's downfall.

First, sinners' wrongdoing will eventually catch up with them, whether sooner or later.

Saul died because of his transgression.

Second, no one's importance or social rank can exempt that person from God's judgments.

Third, disobedience brings death.

Saul died because he did not keep the Lord's word.

May we be delivered from unbelief, impatience and despair.

By waiting for the Lord, we will obtain a kingdom that cannot be shaken.
classic_reading:
[1Chr.10.1]
Chapter 10
The death of Saul.
--The design chiefly in view in these books of the Chronicles, appears to be to preserve the records of the house of David. Therefore the writer repeats not the history of Saul's reign, but only of his death, by which a way was made for David to the throne. And from the ruin of Saul, we may learn, 1. That the sin of sinners will certainly find them out, sooner or later; Saul died for his transgression. 2. That no man's greatness can exempt him from the judgments of God. 3. Disobedience is a killing thing. Saul died for not keeping the word of the Lord. May be delivered from unbelief, impatience, and despair. By waiting on the Lord we shall obtain a kingdom that cannot be moved.
